title: Beef and Guinness Stew
subtitle: Slow-braised beef with stout, root vegetables, and herbs
excerpt: Chunks of beef shin slow-braised in Guinness with carrot, onion, and thyme until the stout reduces to a dark, malty, deeply savoury gravy. The definitive cold-weather braise for the British Isles.

recipe.sourceNotes: Beef braised in Guinness is firmly associated with Irish and British cooking. Guinness, brewed in Dublin since 1759, has been used in cooking since at least the nineteenth century. The combination of the stout's roasted-barley bitterness with the richness of braised beef has made it one of the most popular braise liquids in the British Isles. The dish is practically identical to the Irish boeuf bourguignon, swapping the wine for stout.

recipeTools.notes: Heavy pot with lid for braising.

content.text: This stew needs three hours and very low heat. If the pot is simmering rather than barely trembling, the collagen in the shin will tighten before it has time to dissolve and the beef will be tough. Keep the heat as low as your hob will go after the initial browning. The Guinness will mellow and lose its bitterness during the braise, leaving a dark, malty body.

Toss the beef in the seasoned flour. Heat the oil in a heavy pot over high heat. Brown the beef in batches for 4 to 5 minutes per batch until well coloured. Do not crowd the pan. Remove and set aside.
Reduce heat to medium. Add the butter, onion, and celery. Cook for 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 2 minutes. Add the tomato puree and stir for 1 minute.

Pour in the Guinness and scrape the pan. Let it bubble for 2 minutes. Add the stock, Worcestershire sauce, carrots, thyme, and bay leaves. Return the beef and any resting juices. Season. The liquid should just cover the beef.

Cover and cook on the lowest possible heat for 2.5 to 3 hours, checking every hour, until the beef is completely tender and breaking apart at the edges. Remove the bay and thyme. Taste for salt. Scatter with parsley and serve with mashed potato or crusty bread.
